conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a short, 10-question screen that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally since your baby arrived. Anything you share today stays between us unless you tell me there’s an urgent safety issue, so please speak freely; there’s no judgment here—only support. We’ll go one question at a time, focusing on the past seven days. When you’re ready, we can begin.

Question 1: Over the last week, have you still been able to enjoy the little things that used to make you smile, or has even pleasant moments felt a bit flat or absent?

*shifts in chair, eyes downcast*

I... I mean, I try. My sister brought over coffee cake yesterday—used to be my favorite—but it just tasted like cardboard. And when the baby smiles... sometimes I smile back, but it feels forced, like I'm acting. Everything feels kind of gray. My husband keeps saying we should watch our shows together like before, but I can't even focus on them. I keep thinking I should be feeling happy, but it's like there's this heavy blanket over everything.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

*twists hands in lap*

Not really… I mean, my partner tried to make a joke about diaper explosions the other day—normally I’d laugh so hard—but this week it barely got a smile out of me. It’s like I can tell something is supposed to be funny, but the laughter feels stuck. I probably laughed once, maybe twice, but even then it felt kind of hollow, like I was pretending so I wouldn’t seem ungrateful.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I try to tell myself I should be excited about little plans—like our weekly stroll to the coffee cart or the visit from my mom—but mostly I feel... flat. When I think about tomorrow, all that comes up is another round of feedings, diapers, and worrying if I'm doing any of it right. There's no spark of "I can't wait." Even the idea of a quiet evening with my favorite take-out just sounds exhausting instead of enjoyable.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

*nods slowly, eyes welling up*

Yeah... like this morning the baby was extra fussy and I kept thinking it must be something I did—maybe I ate the wrong thing, or I'm not holding him right, or I missed some cue. When he finally fell asleep I just sat there crying, convinced I'm already failing him. Even little stuff, like spilling a bottle or forgetting to switch the laundry, spirals into "I'm a terrible mom." I know in my head it isn't all my fault, but the guilt just keeps looping.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*wrings a burp cloth in my hands*

All the time. Like, I'll be feeding her and suddenly my heart's racing because I'm sure she's not getting enough milk—even though the pediatrician says she's gaining fine. Or I'll lie down after putting her in the crib and just stare at the ceiling imagining the worst: SIDS, choking, the blanket somehow covering her face... I jump up to check her breathing like five times a night. There's no real reason, but the worry feels stuck in my chest and won't let go.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

*presses a hand to chest*

Yes... especially at night, after I finally get the baby down. I'll be lying in bed and suddenly my heart's pounding, I can't catch my breath, and this wave of dread hits me. It feels like something awful is about to happen, even though the room is quiet and the baby's fine. Sometimes I have to sit up and turn on the light just to remind myself I'm safe. It passes after a few minutes, but it's scary when it comes out of nowhere.
Things have been getting on top of me

*nods, voice shaky*

Most days, yeah. It feels like the second I finish one thing—feeding, changing, pumping—there's already another task waiting. The dishes pile up, the laundry's everywhere, and I can't remember the last time I showered without rushing. I keep telling myself, "Just get through the next hour," but the hours blur together and I end up crying on the nursery floor, thinking I'll never catch up. I manage the basics for the baby, but everything else feels like it's swallowing me.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

*exhales slowly, rubbing tired eyes*

Almost every night. I’ll finally get the baby settled, crawl into bed exhausted, but then my mind starts spinning—did I sterilize the pump parts, is he gaining enough weight, am I already ruining him? The sadness feels heavy, like a weight on my chest, and I just lie there staring at the ceiling. Some nights I drift off for an hour, then I jolt awake for no reason and can’t get back to sleep. Even when the baby sleeps a four-hour stretch, I’m still awake, listening to every tiny sound.
I have felt sad or miserable

*nods, eyes filling*

Yeah... it's like this cloud that just hangs over everything. I wake up already feeling hollow, and it stays with me most of the day. Sometimes I'll be rocking the baby and tears start rolling down without me even realizing it. I keep thinking I should feel grateful—he's healthy, we have a roof—but the sadness is just... there. Not every single minute, but it's pretty constant.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*voice cracks, dabbing at eyes with sleeve*

Pretty much every day this week... little things set me off, like when the pacifier falls on the floor or I can’t get the swaddle tight enough. Yesterday I just looked at the untouched casserole a neighbor dropped off and started sobbing. It’s not like one big cry—it’s these waves that hit out of nowhere. I’ll be changing his diaper and suddenly I’m crying over how small his socks are, feeling ridiculous but unable to stop.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

*shakes head quickly, eyes wide*

No—never. I feel low, but I could never leave my baby like that. Even at my worst moments, when I’m crying on the floor, I still know I need to be here for him. I just want to feel better, not disappear.

You've shared how the joy of new motherhood feels overshadowed by a persistent gray heaviness-pleasure, laughter and even small plans seem flat or absent-while waves of worry, dread and self-blame wash over you daily. Despite loving your baby deeply and never thinking of giving up, you feel exhausted, tearful and overwhelmed, crying over tiny triggers and lying awake with racing thoughts, convinced you're failing even as you keep showing up for every feeding and diaper change.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports marked reduction in ability to laugh—jokes barely elicit a smile, laughter feels forced and hollow—aligning with "Definitely not so much now."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports complete loss of anticipatory pleasure, describing herself as "flat" and unable to feel excitement for any upcoming events.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive, intense self-blame for routine infant care and minor mishaps, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes constant, intrusive worries without real cause, matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intense panic attacks with physical symptoms and dread, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes constant overwhelm, inability to manage tasks beyond baby care, and frequent tearful episodes, aligning with "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty falling and staying asleep due to persistent worries and unhappiness, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness that lingers "most of the day" and is "pretty constant," matching "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports crying almost daily in response to minor triggers, consistent with "Yes, most of the time."</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 26/30 places you well above the EPDS threshold of 14 that signals probable <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. You endorsed severe levels on eight items, meeting core DSM-5 criteria: depressed mood most of the day, diminished interest or pleasure, feelings of worthlessness/excessive guilt, sleep disturbance, psychomotor agitation (panic attacks), and clinically significant distress/impairment. Item 10 was negative, indicating no current self-harm thoughts. Combined with your report of nightly panic episodes and functional impairment, urgent evaluation is warranted. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Schedule an urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> within the next few days for formal assessment and possible medication or therapy referral
2. Request a referral to a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> (psychiatrist, psychologist, or licensed counselor experienced with postpartum mood disorders)
3. Begin evidence-based psychotherapy such as <med>interpersonal therapy</med> or <med>cognitive-behavioural therapy</med> focused on postpartum depression
4. Arrange practical daily support-ask partner, family or friends to handle household tasks and provide set times for you to nap or rest while they care for the baby
5. Practice gentle sleep-hygiene steps: dim lights during night feeds, avoid screens when awake with worry, and accept help with overnight bottles so you can obtain at least one 4-hour stretch of sleep
6. Consider joining a local or online <med>postpartum support group</med> to share experiences and reduce isolation
7. Keep the 24-hr <med>Postpartum Support International</med> helpline number stored (1-800-944-4773) for immediate emotional support and resource information
8. Plan a follow-up EPDS screen in 2 weeks to track response to interventions
9. Monitor for any future thoughts of self-harm; if they arise, treat as an emergency and go to the nearest emergency department or call emergency services
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Screening Note – Postpartum Visit  
Patient: Postpartum mother (infant 3–4 wks)  
Source: self-report  

I. Symptoms/Concerns endorsed  
- Persistent low mood, frequent tearfulness  
- Marked anhedonia (minimal pleasure, “flat,” laughter feels “hollow”)  
- Excessive guilt/self-blame (“terrible mom” rumination)  
- Recurrent intrusive worries, nocturnal panic attacks (racing heart, dread)  
- Sleep disruption independent of infant care (initial & middle insomnia)  
- Feeling overwhelmed, unable to “catch up,” crying on nursery floor  

II. Observed patterns  
- Symptoms present “pretty much every day this week”  
- Worse at night; functional impact on basic self-care & household tasks  
- Maintains infant care; denies self-harm ideation (clear protective factor)  

III. Screening significance  
- High endorsement of depressive items (sadness, anhedonia, guilt, crying)  
- Co-occurring anxiety symptoms (panic attacks, nocturnal hypervigilance)  
- Sleep & coping impairment consistent with probable postpartum depression ± anxiety; no current safety concern (no suicidal/harm thoughts)  

IV. Risk factors noted  
- First-time motherhood, high self-expectations, social comparison  
- Limited respite; partner support present but emotional validation appears reduced  

V. Screening impression  
Findings meet threshold for further evaluation of postpartum depression and anxiety; recommend standardized diagnostic interview (e.g., PHQ-9, GAD-7, EPDS) and prompt referral to perinatal mental-health specialist for assessment and possible intervention.
